## Executive Summary

## The Problem: An Evidence-Starved Scaling Crisis

The global learning crisis remains acute: approximately 70% of 10-year-olds in low- and middle-income countries cannot read and understand an age-appropriate text, a deficit that post-pandemic recovery efforts have only partially addressed [4]. In response, governments and districts have rushed to deploy AI-driven tutoring platforms at national and municipal scale. The 2026 evaluation cycle—covering UK national deployments, Singapore's centralized rollout, and the Newark Public Schools (NPS) district program—reveals a stark asymmetry: **deployment velocity has vastly outpaced causal evidence generation**. As of October 2025, the Research Repository contained over 800 papers on AI in education, yet only 20 rigorously identify the causal effects of AI tools on students and educators—a 2.5% rigor yield [2]. This executive summary synthesizes the 2026 results across three jurisdictions, benchmarks them against traditional classroom and human-tutoring controls, and quantifies equity-gap consequences.

## Key Systems Compared (2026 Deployment Cycle)

| Dimension | UK (National) | Singapore (National) | US – Newark, NJ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deployment model | Third-party provider consortium, school-day embedded | Ministry-curated platform, centralized procurement | District-led + state grant (high-impact tutoring, AI-augmented) |
| Funding context | Post-COVID recovery (catch-up premium) | Long-term EdTech master plan | $400K NJ state grant for 2026–27 [3] |
| Target population | Bottom-quartile / below-benchmark students | Heterogeneous ability bands | Students below state proficiency; prior diagnostic targeting 15th–60th percentile [23] |
| Dosage (reported) | Variable, 60–90 min/week | ~90 min/week | 90 min/week (per Nashville precedent) [23] |
